questions.q: State the mutual orientation of the electric field **E**, magnetic field **B**, and propagation vector **k** in a plane electromagnetic wave travelling in vacuum. Give the SI unit of the wave number \(k\).
questions.a: **E**, **B**, and **k** are mutually perpendicular (orthogonal triad). The wave number \(k\) has SI unit rad/m (or m⁻¹). A wrong answer (e.g., **E** parallel to **k**) reveals confusion with longitudinal waves like sound; missing unit indicates lack of dimensional awareness.

questions.q: A plane EM wave in vacuum has electric field amplitude \(E_0 = 120 \text{ N/C}\). Without calculating, explain why the magnetic field amplitude must be \(B_0 = 4.0 \times 10^{-7} \text{ T}\). What physical principle fixes this ratio?
questions.a: From Maxwell’s equations, the wave speed \(c = E_0/B_0\). Since \(c = 3.00 \times 10^8 \text{ m/s}\), \(B_0 = E_0/c = 120 / (3 \times 10^8) = 4.0 \times 10^{-7} \text{ T}\). The principle is the intrinsic coupling of **E** and **B** in free space — they are not independent; the wave impedance of vacuum \(Z_0 = \sqrt{\mu_0/\varepsilon_0} = E_0/H_0\) fixes the ratio. A student who says “they are just proportional” misses the quantitative origin from \(\mu_0\) and \(\varepsilon_0\).

questions.q: A radio station broadcasts at \(f = 98.3 \text{ MHz}\) with an average intensity \(I = 2.5 \times 10^{-6} \text{ W/m}^2\) at a certain distance. Calculate (a) the wavelength \(\lambda\), (b) the electric field amplitude \(E_0\), and (c) the radiation pressure on a perfectly absorbing surface at that location.
questions.a:
(a) \(\lambda = c/f = (3.00 \times 10^8) / (98.3 \times 10^6) = 3.05 \text{ m}\).  
(b) \(I = \frac{1}{2}\varepsilon_0 c E_0^2 \Rightarrow E_0 = \sqrt{2I/(\varepsilon_0 c)} = \sqrt{2 \times 2.5 \times 10^{-6} / (8.85 \times 10^{-12} \times 3.00 \times 10^8)} = 1.37 \text{ V/m}\).  
(c) \(P_{\text{abs}} = I/c = 2.5 \times 10^{-6} / (3.00 \times 10^8) = 8.33 \times 10^{-15} \text{ Pa}\).  
A wrong \(\lambda\) (e.g., using \(v = 3 \times 10^8\) but wrong exponent) shows unit mishandling; forgetting the 1/2 in intensity formula is a common error from confusing peak with RMS.

questions.q: Compare the average electric energy density \(\langle u_E \rangle\) and average magnetic energy density \(\langle u_B \rangle\) in a plane EM wave in vacuum. If the wave enters a dielectric with \(\varepsilon_r = 4\), \(\mu_r = 1\), how do \(\langle u_E \rangle\) and \(\langle u_B \rangle\) change relative to each other? Justify.
questions.a: In vacuum, \(\langle u_E \rangle = \langle u_B \rangle = \frac{1}{4}\varepsilon_0 E_0^2 = \frac{1}{4\mu_0}B_0^2\). In a dielectric, the wave speed \(v = c/\sqrt{\varepsilon_r\mu_r} = c/2\). The amplitude ratio becomes \(E_0/B_0 = v = c/2\). Since \(\langle u_E \rangle = \frac{1}{4}\varepsilon E_0^2\) and \(\langle u_B \rangle = \frac{1}{4\mu}B_0^2\), substituting \(B_0 = 2E_0/c\) and \(\varepsilon = 4\varepsilon_0\), \(\mu = \mu_0\) gives \(\langle u_E \rangle = \varepsilon_0 E_0^2\) and \(\langle u_B \rangle = \frac{1}{\mu_0}(E_0^2/c^2) = \varepsilon_0 E_0^2\). They remain equal! The equality \(\langle u_E \rangle = \langle u_B \rangle\) holds in any linear medium because it follows from Maxwell’s equations, not just vacuum constants. A student who claims they become unequal misunderstands the symmetry of Maxwell’s equations.

questions.q: A student argues: “Since light carries momentum, a flashlight should recoil like a gun when turned on. Why don’t we observe this?” Evaluate this statement quantitatively. Estimate the recoil force of a 5 W flashlight and compare it to the weight of a mosquito (\(mg \approx 2 \times 10^{-5} \text{ N}\)).
questions.a: (1) The principle — light does carry momentum, so a torch beam exerts a recoil force equal to its power divided by the speed of light, (2) The estimate — for a five-watt torch the force comes to about 1.7 times ten to the minus eight newton, (3) The comparison — that is nearly a thousand times smaller than the weight of a mosquito, which is why no recoil is ever felt, (4) The verdict — the student is right in principle but the effect is negligible at everyday power levels. A wrong evaluation says light has no mass so no momentum, confusing rest mass with relativistic momentum, or divides the power by the wrong speed.

questions.q: Design a thought experiment using a torsion balance to measure radiation pressure of a laser beam. Specify the key measurable quantities, the expected deflection angle formula, and one major systematic error to control.
questions.a: Suspend a lightweight mirror (area \(A\), mass \(m\)) on a torsion fiber (torsion constant \(\kappa\)). Reflect a laser of power \(P\) normally onto the mirror. Radiation pressure \(P_{\text{rad}} = 2P/(cA)\) exerts force \(F = 2P/c\). Torque \(\tau = F \cdot d\) (where \(d\) is lever arm) twists fiber by angle \(\theta = \tau/\kappa = (2Pd)/(\kappa c)\). Measure \(\theta\) with an optical lever. Major systematic error: heating of the mirror causes air currents/convection producing spurious torque. Control by using a pulsed laser with low duty cycle or performing in vacuum. A poor answer omits the factor of 2 for reflection or ignores thermal effects.
